scoring.subdimension_score: Each question measures one subdimension. The chosen option is the subdimension score, a whole number from 0 to 5.
scoring.dont_know: 'I do not know' gives a score of 0 and sets the flag 'insufficient_evidence', as in the chatbot.
scoring.aggregation: Dimension and overall scores, rounding and the report follow the same rules as the chatbot (Sections 2.4 and 2.5).

items.question: How do employees in your organization typically find the data they need?

options.text: Data is very hard or impossible to find. There is no way to locate it, formal or informal, and nobody has seen this as a problem.
Finding data takes a lot of effort, such as many inquiries or searching scattered sources, and whether it works depends on who is searching.
Data is usually found through informal channels, such as asking a colleague who knows it or lists kept by a team, but this depends on specific people.
There is a documented, organization-wide way to find data, such as a data catalog or central inventory, with standard procedures and contact points.
There is an organization-wide data catalog or inventory, and someone responsible checks regularly that it is complete and up to date.
Search results and employee feedback are used to make the data catalog easier to use, and new datasets are added to it automatically when they are created.
I do not know

items.question: How is responsibility for data handled in your organization?

options.text: There is no concept of data ownership. Nobody is responsible for any data, formally or informally, and this has not been seen as a problem.
No one clearly owns the data. Many people use it, and someone takes responsibility only when a problem occurs, so whether data is maintained varies.
Within teams, people generally know who looks after which data, usually whoever created or uses it, but this is not written down and differs between teams.
Every key dataset has an owner, formally assigned and documented according to one standard for the whole organization and tied to roles rather than people.
Owners are formally assigned and documented, and ownership is reviewed regularly, so datasets without an owner or owners who have left are found and fixed.
Assigning an owner is built into how data is created, so every new dataset has an owner from the start, and the rules change when reviews show problems.
I do not know

items.question: How is data quality handled in your organization, and how usable is the data for analysis or AI?

options.text: Data quality is not managed and has not been seen as a problem. Data is so inconsistent that it cannot be used without being rebuilt.
There are no quality rules. Individuals fix problems when they notice them, usually for one task, and data needs extensive manual cleaning before every use.
Some teams have informal rules and basic checks for their own data, but quality differs between teams, and combining data from different systems needs a lot of cleaning.
Documented quality rules apply across the whole organization, with assigned responsibilities, so data from different systems is consistent and needs only limited preparation.
Quality rules are enforced through system controls, such as required fields. Quality is measured against defined targets, and problems are found and corrected.
Recurring quality problems are fixed at their source, and most checks run automatically. Data can be used for analysis or AI without extra preparation.
I do not know

items.question: How do people in your organization approach AI, in their attitude and in their daily work?

options.text: AI is not used or discussed. Employees have no access to AI tools, and openness to AI has not been seen as something that needs attention.
A few individuals try AI tools on their own, often free versions, without permission or guidance; most employees lack the knowledge or confidence to use AI.
Some teams or departments use AI regularly for specific purposes and encourage experimenting, while others remain skeptical or uninvolved, depending on individual managers.
AI is part of regular work across departments, with approved tools and shared guidelines, and employees are invited to propose and test ideas for using AI.
AI is used across the organization, and its adoption and employees' attitudes are tracked, for example through usage data or surveys, so that low adoption is addressed.
Trying out AI is a normal part of everyday work. Employees regularly propose and test new ideas and share with others what worked and what did not.
I do not know

items.question: Who in your organization has the skills to develop or implement AI?

options.text: Nobody inside or outside the organization has skills to develop or implement AI, and nobody has yet seen the need for such skills.
Only a few individuals have AI skills, which they learned on their own. Working with AI is not part of anyone's role or job description.
Some teams have AI specialists, such as data scientists, or work with external experts. They mostly work alone, without involving business experts.
AI roles are defined across the organization, for example a central AI team or AI champions in departments. AI projects combine technical and business expertise.
AI roles are defined, and AI skills are assessed regularly, for example through skills reviews. Gaps are closed through hiring, training or external partners.
There are career paths for AI roles. The way the organization hires, develops and keeps AI experts is adapted based on what works best.
I do not know

items.question: How do employees in your organization learn to work with AI?

options.text: There is no AI training or support. Nobody has considered that employees might need it, so no one plans or offers any learning about AI.
Employees learn about AI on their own, for example from online videos or by trying tools. There is no training, guidance or sharing of experience.
Some teams have occasional learning, for example a workshop or a colleague showing how they use ChatGPT. It is not organized for the whole organization.
All employees have a structured AI training program, such as online courses for their role, and practical guides for the approved tools. Someone is responsible for it.
There is a structured AI training program, and its outcomes are measured. For example, participation and skills before and after training are tracked, and gaps are fixed.
Learning about AI is part of daily work, for example through an AI community or regular sharing sessions, and courses are updated whenever new AI tools appear.
I do not know

items.question: Has your organization defined what it wants to achieve with AI?

options.text: The organization has not defined what it wants to achieve with AI. Leadership is not interested in defining it, and AI is not discussed.
Individuals have their own ideas about what AI could do for the organization, but nothing is defined, and everyone expects something different from AI.
Some leaders or departments have their own goals for AI, for example automating processes in their area. There is no shared ambition for the whole organization.
A documented AI strategy for the whole organization states what role AI should play, for example improving current work or transforming the business. Everyone knows it.
There is a documented AI strategy, and it is reviewed regularly, at least once a year, against progress and changes such as new regulation.
The AI strategy actively shapes the organization's long-term direction. It is updated whenever results or new developments in AI call for it.
I do not know

items.question: How is AI connected to your organization's business goals?

options.text: AI is not connected to any business goals. It is not considered at all, or only as a technical topic, and leadership is not involved.
AI is treated as a technical experiment. Any objectives are vague, such as "become AI-driven", and leadership rarely links AI to business goals.
Some leaders connect AI to goals in their own area, for example better customer service, but there are no measurable targets for the organization.
AI objectives are measurable business targets linked to the strategy, for example "reduce service costs by 20%", with an executive sponsor and a budget.
AI objectives are measurable, and leadership reviews progress against them regularly. When targets are missed, the reasons are found and addressed.
AI objectives are part of every strategic planning cycle. New targets are set based on what earlier AI projects actually achieved for the business.
I do not know

items.question: How does your organization decide which AI ideas to pursue?

options.text: It does not. Nobody has considered where AI could bring value to the organization, so no AI ideas are collected or discussed.
Ideas start ad hoc, from individual interest or from tools that happen to be available, and they are pursued without any assessment.
Teams choose and fund their own AI projects. Each team judges ideas in its own way, and ideas are not compared across the organization.
An organization-wide process assesses ideas against criteria such as business value and feasibility. A designated team or committee decides which ideas receive funding.
The results of AI projects are measured against their expected value. The list of projects is reviewed regularly, and weak projects are adjusted or stopped.
Lessons from past AI projects are used to improve how ideas are selected, and the organization actively searches for new places where AI could help.
I do not know

items.question: How well do your organization's systems support the use of AI?

options.text: The organization's systems are outdated or separate from each other and cannot run AI tools. Nobody has yet considered what would be needed.
The organization offers only basic tools, such as email and file storage, so people use public AI tools on their own. Data is copied by hand.
Some teams have the tools they need for AI, such as a data analysis platform. Other teams do not, and most systems are not connected.
The whole organization works on one common platform with approved AI tools for everyone. Key systems are connected, so data flows between them automatically.
The common platform and its AI tools are monitored, for example for outages, speed, usage and costs. Problems such as slow systems are fixed.
New AI solutions can be set up and expanded automatically when more people need them, and the platform is adapted as new AI needs appear.
I do not know

items.question: How does your organization obtain AI tools and solutions?

options.text: The organization has not obtained any AI tools or solutions, and nobody has considered how it would choose or buy them.
Individuals choose AI tools themselves, often free versions, without any approval. Nobody checks whether a tool is safe or fits existing systems.
Teams buy or build their own AI solutions and sometimes compare options. Decisions differ between teams and are not coordinated across the organization.
A common approach evaluates tools and vendors against defined criteria, such as cost and security. Approved tools and contracts are managed centrally.
Approved tools and vendors are monitored, for example their costs, license use and performance against the contract. Problems with vendors are addressed.
Experience with vendors and tools is used to update the selection criteria, and decisions to build or buy are reviewed as needs change.
I do not know

items.question: How does your organization protect its data when employees use AI tools?

options.text: There are no rules for protecting data when AI is used. Anyone can enter confidential or personal data into any AI tool, and nobody sees a risk.
A few people protect sensitive data on their own, for example by not pasting customer data into AI tools. There are no rules or access controls.
Some teams have their own rules, for example a list of allowed AI tools or limits on access to data. Other teams have none, and nobody checks.
An organization-wide policy defines which data may be used in which AI tools. Data is classified by sensitivity, and people get access only to what they need.
Access to data and the use of AI tools are reviewed regularly, including compliance with laws such as GDPR. Problems that are found are fixed.
Lessons from reviews, incidents and new laws are used to update the security rules. Monitoring is largely automated, for example alerts for sensitive data.
